claim: Virtually all species of coelomate animals contain blood cells that display a division of labor necessary for homeostasis.
source: Virtually all species of coelomate animals contain blood cells that display a division of labor necessary for homeostasis.
evidence: This is a general statement about animal biology presented in the introduction without specific experimental data from this study, but draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, the lymph gland produces plasmatocytes and crystal cells that are not released until pupariation.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, the lymph gland produces plasmatocytes and crystal cells that are not released until pupariation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Throughout larval development, both hemocyte types (plasmatocytes and crystal cells) increase in numbers.
source: Yet, throughout larval development, both hemocyte types increase in numbers.
evidence: This is a known observation in the field that sets up the research question.

claim: Mature plasmatocytes can proliferate.
source: Mature plasmatocytes can proliferate but it is not known if crystal cell numbers increase by self-renewal or by de novo differentiation.
evidence: This statement is based on prior knowledge in the field.

claim: New crystal cells in third instar larvae originate through a Notch-dependent process of plasmatocyte transdifferentiation.
source: We show that new crystal cells in third instar larvae originate through a Notch-dependent process of plasmatocyte transdifferentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including RNAi experiments and live imaging.

claim: Crystal cell differentiation occurs in the sessile clusters.
source: This process occurs in the sessile clusters and is contingent upon the integrity of these structures.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental observations including video analysis and cluster disruption experiments.

claim: Crystal cell differentiation is contingent upon the integrity of sessile cluster structures.
source: This process occurs in the sessile clusters and is contingent upon the integrity of these structures.
evidence: This is supported by cluster disruption experiments showing reduced crystal cell differentiation when clusters are disrupted.

claim: Insect hemocyte functions include phagocytosis, extracellular matrix deposition, AMP production, encapsulation, and melanization.
source: In insects, the functions of hemocytes (blood cells) are very diverse and include phagocytosis, extracellular matrix deposition, AMP production, encapsulation, and melanization.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Honti et al., 2014.

claim: Different functions performed by insect hemocytes are compartmentalized into different cell types.
source: Similarly to what happens in vertebrates, the different functions performed by insect hemocytes are, to some degree, compartmentalized into different cell types (Honti et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Some mature blood cells retain the ability to divide when in circulation.
source: Some mature blood cells retain the ability to divide when in circulation, but the majority of blood cell proliferation and differentiation occurs in the hematopoietic organs (Grigorian and Hartenstein, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation.

claim: The majority of blood cell proliferation and differentiation occurs in the hematopoietic organs.
source: Some mature blood cells retain the ability to divide when in circulation, but the majority of blood cell proliferation and differentiation occurs in the hematopoietic organs (Grigorian and Hartenstein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hematopoietic organs provide the correct cellular and molecular environment for the control of cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: These organs provide the correct cellular and molecular environment for the control of cell proliferation and differentiation, namely in the so-called stem cell niches (Koch and Radtke, 2007; Martinez-Agosto et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Embryonic hematopoiesis in Drosophila melanogaster produces two different types of mature hemocytes: plasmatocytes and crystal cells.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, embryonic hematopoiesis produces two different types of mature hemocytes: plasmatocytes and crystal cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Plasmatocytes are phagocytic cells often functionally compared to vertebrate macrophages.
source: Plasmatocytes are phagocytic cells often functionally compared to vertebrate macrophages (Evans et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Crystal cells are non-phagocytic cells known to produce prophenoloxidase, an essential component of the melanization cascade.
source: Crystal cells are non-phagocytic cells known to produce prophenoloxidase, an essential component of the melanization cascade (Binggeli et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Both plasmatocytes and crystal cells generated during embryogenesis persist into larval stages.
source: Both plasmatocytes and crystal cells generated during embryogenesis persist into larval stages.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The majority of hemocytes in the larva are attached to the cuticular epidermis as sessile cells.
source: Hemocytes in the larva can be found in circulation but the majority of them are attached to the cuticular epidermis as sessile cells (Lanot et al., 2001; Kurucz et al., 2007b; Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Hemocytes attached to the epidermis form stereotypical clusters of cells in every segment of the larva.
source: Hemocytes attached to the epidermis are not randomly dispersed but form stereotypical clusters of cells in every segment of the larva (Zettervall et al., 2004; Makhijani et al., 2011) indicating that some signal must direct hemocytes to these locations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Some signal must direct hemocytes to form clusters at specific locations.
source: Hemocytes attached to the epidermis are not randomly dispersed but form stereotypical clusters of cells in every segment of the larva (Zettervall et al., 2004; Makhijani et al., 2011) indicating that some signal must direct hemocytes to these locations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the stereotypical pattern of cluster formation.

claim: Peripheral nervous system (PNS) neurons attract hemocytes and provide unknown trophic molecules for their survival.
source: In fact, it has been recently shown that peripheral nervous system (PNS) neurons attract hemocytes and provide unknown trophic molecules for their survival (Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The lymph gland is a hematopoietic organ where plasmatocytes and crystal cells differentiate from prohemocytes.
source: The larva also possesses a hematopoietic organ, the lymph gland, where plasmatocytes and crystal cells differentiate from prohemocytes (Crozatier and Meister, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Prohemocytes in the medullary zone of the lymph gland are instructed by cells from the posterior signaling center (PSC) to maintain their quiescent state or to differentiate.
source: Prohemocytes residing in the medullary zone of the lymph gland are instructed by cells from the posterior signaling center (PSC) to maintain their quiescent state or to differentiate into mature plasmatocytes or crystal cells (Crozatier et al., 2004; Mandal et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During differentiation in the lymph gland, cells migrate and occupy the most cortical zone.
source: During the differentiation process, it has been suggested that cells migrate and occupy the most cortical zone of the lymph gland (Jung et al., 2005; Krzemien et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Hemocytes produced in the lymph gland do not disperse from the organ until pupariation or upon injury such as parasitoid wasp egg infection.
source: An essential aspect of the Drosophila larval hematopoiesis is that hemocytes produced in the lymph gland do not disperse from the organ until pupariation or upon injury such as parasitoid wasp egg infection (Holz et al., 2003; Honti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In homeostatic conditions, differentiated hemocytes in the lymph gland do not contribute to the circulating and sessile hemocyte population.
source: Hence, in homeostatic conditions, differentiated hemocytes in the lymph gland do not contribute to the circulating and sessile hemocyte population.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that lymph gland hemocytes are not released until pupariation.

claim: The hemocyte population found in circulation and in sessile patches expands throughout larval development.
source: Nonetheless, the hemocyte population found in circulation and in sessile patches expands throughout larval development.
evidence: This is established knowledge that motivates the research question.

claim: Plasmatocytes are mitotically active cells expanding during larval development by self renewal.
source: Plasmatocytes are mitotically active cells (Rizki, 1957; Lanot et al., 2001) expanding during larval development by self renewal (Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mature crystal cells do not divide during larval stages.
source: On the other hand, all reports thus far concur in that mature crystal cells do not divide during larval stages (Krzemien et al., 2010b; Lanot et al., 2001; Rizki, 1957), although they have been shown to proliferate during embryogenesis (Lebestky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Crystal cells have been shown to proliferate during embryogenesis.
source: On the other hand, all reports thus far concur in that mature crystal cells do not divide during larval stages (Krzemien et al., 2010b; Lanot et al., 2001; Rizki, 1957), although they have been shown to proliferate during embryogenesis (Lebestky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Notch signaling is necessary to form crystal cells.
source: Although little is known on how crystal cells are formed outside the lymph gland, it has been shown that Notch signaling is necessary to form these cells (Duvic et al., 2002; Lebestky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the lymph gland, the role of Notch signaling in crystal cell formation is cell autonomous.
source: In the lymph gland, the role of Notch signaling in crystal cell formation is cell autonomous (Mukherjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Notch activation is sufficient in hemocytes to induce the expression of lozenge.
source: Notch activation is sufficient in hemocytes to induce the expression of lozenge, the first known transcription factor in crystal cell development (Lebestky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lozenge is the first known transcription factor in crystal cell development.
source: Notch activation is sufficient in hemocytes to induce the expression of lozenge, the first known transcription factor in crystal cell development (Lebestky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Notch signaling requires cell contact since the two known Drosophila Notch ligands, Serrate and Delta, are membrane bound proteins.
source: One particularity of Notch signaling is that it requires cell contact since the two known Drosophila Notch ligands, Serrate and Delta, are membrane bound proteins (Fiúza and Arias, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In the lymph gland, Serrate-positive hemocytes induce neighboring cells to adopt crystal cell fates.
source: In the lymph gland, Serrate-positive hemocytes induce neighboring cells to adopt crystal cell fates (Lebestky et al., 2003; Mukherjee et al., 2011; Ferguson & Martinez-agosto 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Only in sessile clusters may we observe hemocytes establishing stable cell–cell contacts between them outside the lymph gland.
source: Outside the lymph gland, only in sessile clusters may we observe hemocytes establishing stable cell–cell contacts between them (Lanot et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hemocytes in clusters are densely packed and linked through interdigitations.
source: In fact, hemocytes in clusters are densely packed and linked through interdigitations (Lanot et al., 2001), particularly in the last two abdominal larval segments, the putative posterior hematopoietic tissue (PHT) (Kurucz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Hemocytes taken from sessile clusters have the ability to differentiate into lamellocytes upon transfer to a different larva.
source: Firstly, in a descriptive endeavor by Kurucz et al. (2007) where an operational posterior hematopoietic tissue (PHT) consisting of the sessile hemocyte clusters in the last two abdominal segments is postulated; and later in a set of experiments showing that hemocytes taken from these clusters have the ability to differentiate into lamellocytes upon transfer to a different larva (Márkus et al., 2009; Honti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sessile hemocytes in clusters constitute the biggest compartment of hemocytes in the larva.
source: Importantly, sessile hemocytes in clusters constitute the biggest compartment of hemocytes in the larva (Lanot et al., 2001; Makhijani et al., 2011), contained within epidermal and muscle tissue in a structure that has been called hematopoietic pockets (Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sessile plasmatocytes in clusters have a higher division rate than those in circulation.
source: Moreover, the sessile plasmatocytes in such clusters have a higher division rate than those in circulation (Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: It is possible to distinguish Hml+Lz− from Hml+Lz+ sessile hemocytes across the larval cuticle using HemolectinΔ-nuclearDsRed and Lozenge-GAL4 in combination with UAS-EGFP/mCD8GFP.
source: With this combination of markers we can distinguish across the larval cuticle, Hml+Lz− from Hml+Lz+ sessile hemocytes (Figure 1A,A′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the images in Figure 1A and A'.

claim: Lozenge expression is maintained as the crystal cell matures.
source: Lozenge is the first marker known in the genetic cascade that leads to crystal cell differentiation and its expression is maintained as the cell matures (Lebestky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hml+Lz+ cells are fully mature crystal cells or differentiating crystal cells while Hml+Lz− cells are plasmatocytes.
source: Hence, Hml+Lz+ cells are fully mature crystal cells or differentiating crystal cells while Hml+Lz− cells are plasmatocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known expression patterns of these markers.

claim: During maturation, crystal cells lose HmlΔ-GAL4 expression.
source: During maturation, crystal cells loose HmlΔ-GAL4 expression (Mukherjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The same loss of expression is observed with HmlΔ-nuclearDsRed but only in rare cells.
source: The same is observed with HmlΔ-nuclearDsRed but only in rare cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the current study.

claim: The difference in frequency of Hml− cells between HmlΔ-GAL4 and HmlΔ-nuclearDsRed may be explained by the different degradation times of nuclearDsRed and cytoplasmatic GFP.
source: This difference may be explained by the different degradation times of nuclearDsRed and cytoplasmatic GFP.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed difference.

claim: It is possible to detect a higher proportion of Hml−Lz+ cells with HmlΔ-cytoplasmaticDsRed.
source: In fact, it is possible to detect a higher proportion of Hml−Lz+ cells with HmlΔ-cytoplasmaticDsRed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Plasmatocytes tend to increase in size as they mature.
source: Another characteristic that distinguishes plasmatocytes from crystal cells is that the former tend to increase in size as they mature (Terriente-Felix et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There is a clear difference in size distributions between Hml+Lz−, Hml+Lz+, and Hml−Lz+ cells.
source: Measuring hemocytes cell areas in the three different populations of cells, we can observe a clear difference in size distributions between Hml+Lz−, Hml+Lz+, and Hml−Lz+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both plasmatocytes and crystal cell numbers increase during larval development.
source: When quantifying total hemocyte counts throughout larva development, it is undisputed that both plasmatocytes and crystal cell numbers increase (Rizki, 1957; Lanot et al., 2001; Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The majority of larval hemocytes are originated during third instar larval development.
source: Here, we focus on third instar larvae because this is the developmental window in which the majority of larval hemocytes are originated (Lanot et al., 2001; Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Hml+ cells increase as third instar larval development proceeds, both in males and females.
source: We could confirm that Hml+ cells increase as third instar larval development proceeds, both in males and females (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The number of Lz+ cells increases during third instar larval development.
source: The number of Lz+ cells also increases in the same time period (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In females there is no difference in the number of Lz+ cells in the last 16 hr of third instar development.
source: In females there is no difference in the number of Lz+ in the last 16 hr of development.
evidence: This is an observation from the data in Figure 1B.

claim: Late third stage larva females have less crystal cells than males.
source: With this, late third stage larva females have less crystal cells than males which is not common in the majority of fly stocks where females tend to have a higher number of crystal cells than males (see 'Results' below).
evidence: This is an observation from the data that is noted as unusual.

claim: Committed crystal cells (Hml+Lz+) are increasing in number during third instar larval development, in parallel with an expansion of the plasmatocyte (Hml+Lz−) population.
source: Nevertheless, the results clearly show that committed crystal cells (Hml+Lz+) are increasing in number during third instar larval development, in parallel with an expansion of the plasmatocyte (Hml+Lz−) population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data in Figure 1B.

claim: Approximately 7% of Hml+Lz− cells divide during a 3-hour period in early L3 larvae.
source: Throughout this 3-hr period, we estimate that ∼7% of Hml+Lz− cells divide (n = 13 videos with mean 50 Hml+Lz− and 6 Hml+Lz+ cells per video).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from time-lapse videos.

claim: No case of Hml+Lz+ cell division was seen in any video.
source: No case of Hml+Lz+ cell division was seen in any video.
evidence: This is based on direct observation from time-lapse videos.

claim: Hml+Lz+ sessile cells in dorsal clusters divide at an extremely low frequency or are post mitotic cells.
source: This suggests that Hml+Lz+ sessile cells in dorsal clusters divide at an extremely low frequency or are post mitotic cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of observed divisions in the videos.

claim: Plasmatocytes (Hml+Lz−) proliferate within sessile clusters.
source: In contrast, we confirm that plasmatocytes (Hml+Lz−) proliferate within sessile clusters as previously reported (Honti et al., 2010; Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is confirmed by video observations and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It was possible to see induction of GFP in GFP− cells, demonstrating that an Hml+Lz− cell is turning into an Hml+Lz+ cell.
source: Notably, it was possible to see induction of GFP in GFP− cells, demonstrating that an Hml+Lz− cell is turning into an Hml+Lz+ cell (Arrowhead in Figure 1C) (see Video 1).
evidence: This is based on direct observation from time-lapse videos shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: Cells that start with low lozenge expression tend to increase it with time.
source: During our analysis cells that start with low expression tend to increase it with time (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Larger Hml+Lz+ cells have more GFP, measured by mean grey value.
source: When we bleed larvae and analyze Hml+Lz+ cells, we also see a tendency for larger cells to have more GFP, measured by mean grey value of the picture (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Lozenge expression starts in Hml+Lz− cells morphologically indistinct from plasmatocytes and increases together with cell size as crystal cell maturation progresses.
source: In conjugation, these results indicate that lozenge expression starts in Hml+Lz− cells morphologically indistinct from plasmatocytes and increases together with cell size as crystal cell maturation progresses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple observations including video analysis and cell size measurements.

claim: During the first 24 hr after third instar ecdysis Hml+Lz− increase approximately 1.4× while Hml+Lz+ increase approximately 2.7×.
source: During the first 24 hr after third instar ecdysis Hml+Lz− increase ∼1.4× while Hml+Lz+ increase ∼2.7× (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on quantification shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The proportion of Hml+Lz+-induced cells in the videos is approximately 3.5% in 3 hr.
source: The proportion of Hml+Lz+-induced cells in our videos is ∼3.5% in 3 hr.
evidence: This is based on quantification from video analysis.

claim: The differentiation rate calculated from video analysis is sufficient to explain the increase in Hml+Lz+ cell number observed in the first 24 hr of third instar larval development.
source: The differentiation rate calculated in our video analysis is sufficient to explain the increase in Hml+Lz+ cell number observed in the first 24 hr of third instar larval development.
evidence: This is based on mathematical extrapolation from the observed differentiation rate.

claim: The mean increase of Lz+ cells measured during development is 256.4 cells.
source: The mean increase of Lz+ cells measured during development is 256.4 cells (Figure 1B) and the extrapolation gives an increase of 447 Lz+ cells.
evidence: This is based on data from Figure 1B.

claim: The extrapolation from video analysis gives an increase of 447 Lz+ cells.
source: The mean increase of Lz+ cells measured during development is 256.4 cells (Figure 1B) and the extrapolation gives an increase of 447 Lz+ cells.
evidence: This is based on mathematical extrapolation from video data.

claim: Hml+Lz+ cells differentiate from Hml+Lz− cells in hemocyte clusters at a rate that is sufficient to explain the increase in this cell type observed in the first 24 hr of L3 development.
source: On the whole, the analysis of these videos shows that Hml+Lz+ cells differentiate from Hml+Lz− cells in hemocyte clusters at a rate that is sufficient to explain the increase in this cell type observed in the first 24 hr of L3 development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on video analysis and mathematical extrapolation.

claim: During lymph gland development, Nimrod is only detectable in mature plasmatocytes and it is not expressed in Lz+ cells.
source: During lymph gland development, Nimrod is only detectable in mature plasmatocytes and it is not expressed in Lz+ cells (Terriente-Felix et al., 2013; Ferguson & Martinez-agosto 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the lymph gland, Lz+ cells differentiate from Hml+Nimrod− cells.
source: Thus, in the lymph gland Lz+ cells differentiate from Hml+Nimrod− cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression patterns of these markers in the lymph gland.

claim: The majority of Lz+ sessile cells are also Nimrod+.
source: Contrarily to the lymph gland, the majority of Lz+ cells are also Nimrod+ (Figure 2A–A″).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A-A''.

claim: Lz+ cells differentiate from a pool of mature plasmatocytes in sessile clusters.
source: This result suggests that Lz+ cells differentiate from a pool of mature plasmatocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Lz+ cells are Nimrod+.

claim: Crystal cells burst after bleeding.
source: It is worth noticing that, because crystal cells burst after bleeding (Bidla et al., 2007), there is a bias in immunofluorescence stainings in favor of more immature crystal cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Plasmatocytes transdifferentiate into lamellocytes.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown before that plasmatocytes transdifferentiate into lamellocytes (Honti et al., 2010; Meister and Ferrandon, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During plasmatocyte to lamellocyte transdifferentiation, cells that are phagocytically active become non-phagocytic and start to express lamellocyte markers.
source: In this case, cells that are phagocytically active become non-phagocytic and start to express lamellocyte markers (Honti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Phagocytosis index is higher in Lz− hemocytes but it is still non-negligible in Lz+ hemocytes.
source: From our results, it is evident that phagocytosis index is higher in Lz− hemocytes but it is still non-negligible in Lz+ hemocytes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by phagocytosis assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The smaller and GFPlow expressing Lz+ cells are able to phagocyte bacteria.
source: When we characterize cell area and GFP intensity in Lz+ cells, it is possible to observe that the smaller and GFPlow expressing cells are able to phagocyte bacteria (Figure 2B′).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B'.

claim: Large cells that have GFPhigh expression are virtually non-phagocytic cells.
source: Large cells that have GFPhigh expression are virtually non-phagocytic cells.
evidence: This is based on the phagocytosis assay data.

claim: Induced Lz+ cells are plasmatocytes with phagocytic activity, which is lost as they mature into crystal cells.
source: This indicates that induced Lz+ cells are plasmatocytes with phagocytic activity, which is lost as they mature into crystal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phagocytosis data showing a correlation between GFP intensity/cell size and phagocytic capacity.

claim: These results support the transdifferentiation of mature phagocytically active plasmatocytes into non-phagocytic crystal cells.
source: Altogether, these results support the transdifferentiation of mature phagocytically active plasmatocytes into non-phagocytic crystal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including Nimrod expression and phagocytosis data.

claim: Crystal cell numbers are reduced in larvae raised at a restrictive temperature in a thermo sensitive Notch allele background.
source: As mentioned above, crystal cell numbers are reduced in larvae raised at a restrictive temperature in a thermo sensitive Notch allele background (Duvic et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The reduction in crystal cells in Notch mutants is visible in sessile hemocytes and in the lymph gland.
source: This reduction is visible in sessile hemocytes and in the lymph gland (Duvic et al., 2002; Lebestky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the lymph gland Notch signaling has a cell autonomous role on Hml+Lz− cells.
source: In the lymph gland Notch signaling has a cell autonomous role on Hml+Lz− cells (Mukherjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Notch downregulation reduces the number of sessile crystal cells both in females and males.
source: Firstly, we establish that Notch downregulation reduces the number of sessile crystal cells both in females (Figure 3A) and males (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only Serrate mutants have reduced numbers of embryonically derived crystal cells.
source: Only Serrate mutants have reduced numbers of embryonically derived crystal cell (Duvic et al., 2002; Lebestky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Knocking down Serrate in hemocytes reduces the number of crystal cells to a similar level than found using Notch RNAi, as opposed to disrupting Delta function.
source: Similarly, knocking down Serrate in hemocytes (HmlΔ-GAL4>UAS-Serrate RNAi) reduces the number of crystal cells to a similar level than found using Notch RNAi, as opposed to disrupting Delta function (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Serrate, the ligand necessary to induce Notch signaling in hemocytes, is expressed in the hemocytes themselves.
source: This indicates that Serrate, the ligand necessary to induce Notch signaling in hemocytes, interestingly, it is expressed in the hemocytes themselves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi experiments showing that Serrate knockdown in hemocytes reduces crystal cell numbers.

claim: The knockdown of Notch does not disrupt the hemocyte clusters.
source: Importantly, the knockdown of Notch does not disrupt the hemocyte clusters nor changes the concentration of hemocytes in circulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2,3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: The knockdown of Notch does not change the concentration of hemocytes in circulation.
source: Importantly, the knockdown of Notch does not disrupt the hemocyte clusters nor changes the concentration of hemocytes in circulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2,3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: Notch enhancer GFP reporters can be detected in Lz+ sessile hemocytes.
source: As observed in the lymph gland (Terriente-Felix et al., 2013), we can detect Notch enhancer GFP reporters in Lz+ sessile hemocytes and, using video analysis, we can observe induction of lozenge in Notch activated cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citation to prior work.

claim: Induction of lozenge can be observed in Notch activated cells using video analysis.
source: As observed in the lymph gland (Terriente-Felix et al., 2013), we can detect Notch enhancer GFP reporters in Lz+ sessile hemocytes and, using video analysis, we can observe induction of lozenge in Notch activated cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by video data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The proportion of Lz+ cells is reduced when Notch expression is inhibited in all hemocytes.
source: To confirm that Notch knockdown inhibits the induction of lozenge in sessile hemocytes and not the maturation of Lz+ cells into crystal cells, we measured the proportion of Lz+ cells with anti-Lozenge antibody while inhibiting Notch expression in all hemocytes (HmlΔ-GAL4>NotchRNAi). The proportion of Lz+ cells in this case is clearly reduced (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Notch knockdown does not significantly increase hemocyte apoptosis.
source: Because increased crystal cell apoptosis could also explain the reduced crystal cell numbers, we estimated hemocyte apoptosis upon Notch knockdown and could not find any significant difference to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Notch activation is essential to induce lozenge expression in larval hemocytes that will mature into crystal cells.
source: Altogether these results confirm that Notch activation is essential to induce lozenge expression in larval hemocytes that will mature into crystal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including RNAi experiments and reporter analysis.

claim: Serrate knockdown with the Lz-GAL4 driver does not reduce the number of crystal cells.
source: To test these alternatives, we performed knockdown of Serrate with the Lz-GAL4 driver and found no reduction in the number of crystal cells (Females in Figure 3D, males in Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Eater-GAL4 and Pxn-GAL4 drivers reduce the number of sessile crystal cells when driving Serrate RNAi.
source: In addition, two other GAL4 drivers expressed in plasmatocytes, Eater-GAL4 and Pxn-GAL4, reduce the number of sessile crystal cells when driving Serrate RNAi (females in Figure 3D, males in Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Plasmatocytes are responsible for Serrate signaling to activate Notch in other plasmatocytes and start crystal cell development.
source: Hence, we conclude that plasmatocyte are responsible for Serrate signaling to activate Notch in other plasmatocytes and start crystal cell development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of Serrate RNAi driven by different GAL4 drivers.

claim: The probability of an Hml+ cell to be also Lz+ increases with the number of cell contacts it establishes with Hml+Lz− cells.
source: If this is the case, we can predict that the probability of an Hml+ cell to be also Lz+ increases with the number of cell contacts it establishes with Hml+Lz− cells. We quantified the number of cell contacts that each cell type makes within the sessile clusters and compared cells within the same size range (i.e., limited to the maximum size of Hml+Lz− cells). As predicted, the proportion of Hml+Lz+/ Hml+Lz− increases with the number of Hml+Lz− cells with which it is in contact (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The proportion of Hml+Lz+/Hml+Lz− increases with the number of Hml+Lz− cells with which it is in contact.
source: As predicted, the proportion of Hml+Lz+/ Hml+Lz− increases with the number of Hml+Lz− cells with which it is in contact (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: After physical manipulation to disrupt clusters, hemocytes start to aggregate again gradually.
source: By rolling groups of larvae between two cover slides, it is possible to force the hemocytes to detach from the epidermis and enter hemolymph circulation. After cluster disruption, hemocytes start to aggregate again, gradually (Makhijani et al., 2011) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: The relative number of Hml+Lz+ cells decreases when clusters are disrupted for 10 hours.
source: Using flow cytometry, we measured the proportion of Hml+Lz+/Hml+Lz− cells at the end of this treatment. The relative number of Hml+Lz+ cells decreases in the treatment group (Figure 4B), indicating that clusters are necessary for crystal cell differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Clusters are necessary for crystal cell differentiation.
source: The relative number of Hml+Lz+ cells decreases in the treatment group (Figure 4B), indicating that clusters are necessary for crystal cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cluster disruption experiment.

claim: Cluster disruption does not significantly change the rate of apoptosis.
source: Firstly, using a PI exclusion assay, we determined if the rate of apoptosis changes upon cluster disruption. There is no significant difference between control and treatment groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by PI exclusion assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cluster disruption does not cause detectable lymph gland-derived hemocytes to enter circulation.
source: When the same technique is used in cluster-disrupted larvae, there is no detectable lymph gland-derived hemocytes in circulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The integrity of the cluster is necessary for crystal cell differentiation.
source: Thus, the integrity of the cluster is necessary for crystal cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cluster disruption experiments.

claim: In Eater mutants that do not form hemocyte clusters, sessile crystal cells are absent.
source: Strikingly, in agreement with our observations, recent work shows that in Eater mutants that do not form hemocyte clusters, sessile crystal cells are absent (Bretscher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work that corroborates the findings.

claim: Notch signaling is necessary for crystal cell differentiation and depends on cluster structure.
source: Altogether these results support that Notch signaling is necessary for crystal cell differentiation and depends on cluster structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including RNAi experiments and cluster disruption experiments.

claim: Lz+ cells have been reported to proliferate during embryogenesis.
source: Lz+ cells have been reported to proliferate during embryogenesis (Lebestky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Lozenge induction in Hml+Lz− is sufficient to explain the increase in Hml+ Lz+ cells during third instar larva.
source: Although, with our results, we cannot exclude that a small proportion of Lz+ cells proliferate during larval stages, we can show that lozenge induction in Hml+Lz− is sufficient to explain the increase in Hml+ Lz+ cells during third instar larva.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on video analysis and mathematical extrapolation.

claim: The activation of lozenge in hemocytes is Notch-dependent with Serrate acting as the ligand.
source: The activation of lozenge in hemocytes is Notch-dependent with Serrate acting as the ligand (Duvic et al., 2002; Lebestky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When serrate expression is ablated only in hemocytes, the number of differentiated crystal cells is severely reduced within the sessile population.
source: When we ablate serrate expression only in hemocytes using the HmlΔ-GAL4 driver coupled to a UAS-SerRNAi, the number of differentiated crystal cells is severely reduced within the sessile population.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi experimental data.

claim: Hemocytes are the cells responsible for crystal cell induction in sessile clusters.
source: This indicates that hemocytes are the cells responsible for crystal cell induction in sessile clusters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RNAi experiments.

claim: The hemocytes inducing crystal cell development are themselves Lz− because SerrateRNAi driven by Lz-GAL4 driver does not decrease the number of crystal cells.
source: Moreover, the hemocytes inducing crystal cell development are themselves Lz− because SerrateRNAi driven by Lz-GAL4 driver does not decrease the number of crystal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of Serrate RNAi with different drivers.

claim: For Notch to be activated it requires that a Serrate expressing cell is in contact for a certain period of time.
source: For Notch to be activated it requires that a Serrate expressing cell is in contact for a certain period of time (Guruharsha et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Hml+Lz+ cells are induced from Hml+Lz− cells in the clusters where contact occurs.
source: We show that this contact is a property of the clusters where Hml+Lz+ cells are induced from Hml+Lz− cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including contact analysis and cluster disruption experiments.

claim: In both sessile clusters and lymph gland, the precursor to a crystal cell is an Hml+Lz− hemocyte.
source: This observation establishes an important parallel between sessile and lymph gland crystal cell development. In both cases, the precursor to a crystal cell is an Hml+Lz− hemocyte (Mukherjee et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current findings and citation to prior work.

claim: Hemocytes only activate lozenge expression in the cortical zone of the lymph gland.
source: Although hemocytes only activate lozenge expression in the cortical zone of the lymph gland (Lebestky et al., 2000), the work of Krzemien et al. suggest that in the medullary zone of the lymph gland cells are already committed to become crystal cells at late second instar (Krzemien et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the medullary zone of the lymph gland cells are already committed to become crystal cells at late second instar.
source: Although hemocytes only activate lozenge expression in the cortical zone of the lymph gland (Lebestky et al., 2000), the work of Krzemien et al. suggest that in the medullary zone of the lymph gland cells are already committed to become crystal cells at late second instar (Krzemien et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Medullary zone cells migrating to the cortical zone can be considered pro-crystal cells.
source: This suggests that medullary zone cells migrating to the cortical zone can be considered pro-crystal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited work about lymph gland development.

claim: In the lymph gland, no co-localization between plasmatocyte marker P1 and crystal cell marker Lz is ever observed.
source: In line with this observation, in the lymph gland, no co-localization between plasmatocyte marker P1 and crystal cell marker Lz is ever observed (Terriente-Felix et al., 2013; Ferguson & Martinez-agosto 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Analyses in hemocyte clusters suggest that lozenge induction occurs in mature plasmatocytes.
source: In contrast, our analyses in hemocyte clusters suggest that lozenge induction occurs in mature plasmatocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence from the current study.

claim: Lz+ cells derive from P1+ cells.
source: Firstly, they derive from P1 cells.
evidence: This is based on the immunofluorescence data showing P1 expression in Lz+ cells.

claim: Lz+GFPlow cells can phagocyte as opposed to Lz+GFPhigh cells, which lose this capacity.
source: Secondly, Lz+GFPlow cells can phagocyte as opposed to Lz+GFPhigh cells, which loose this capacity.
evidence: This is based on the phagocytosis assay data.

claim: Lz+GFPlow cells are the initial stages of crystal cell differentiation as virtually all Lz+GFPlow become Lz+GFPhigh.
source: Lz+GFPlow cells are, according to our video analysis, the initial stages of crystal cell differentiation as virtually all Lz+GFPlow become Lz+GFPhigh.
evidence: This is based on video analysis observations.

claim: Throughout time cells increase their GFP expression and become larger.
source: Throughout time cells increase their GFP expression and become larger.
evidence: This is based on video analysis and cell size measurements.

claim: Mature plasmatocytes can differentiate into crystal cells.
source: Altogether our results suggest that mature plasmatocytes can differentiate into crystal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claim: Circulating crystal cells in the larva derive from cells that express the plasmatocyte-specific marker croquemort during the embryonic stage.
source: Firstly, circulating crystal cells in the larva derive from cells that express the plasmatocyte-specific marker croquemort during the embryonic stage (Franc et al., 1999; Honti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Lebestky et al. consider that a small fraction of the Lz-GAL4 positive cells gives rise to plasmatocytes defined by morphology and croquemort expression.
source: Secondly, Lebestky et al. consider that a small fraction of the Lz-GAL4 positive cells gives rise to plasmatocytes defined by morphology and croquemort expression (Lebestky et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The plasmatocyte-like cells expressing lozenge are plasmatocytes in route to become crystal cells.
source: In light of our results, we propose that the plasmatocyte-like cells expressing lozenge are plasmatocytes in route to become crystal cells.
evidence: This is a reinterpretation of prior observations in light of the current findings.

claim: The hypothesis that plasmatocytes give rise to crystal cells was put forward by Rizky in 1957.
source: To our knowledge, the hypothesis that plasmatocytes give rise to crystal cells was put forward by Rizky in 1957, with the purpose of explaining how crystal cells increase in number without proliferation (Rizki, 1957).
evidence: This is a historical reference to prior work.

claim: Hemocyte clusters work as a true hematopoietic tissue.
source: Yet, with the results shown here, we propose that hemocyte clusters work as a true hematopoietic tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The presence and integrity of hemocyte clusters are necessary for the proper establishment of Hml+Lz+/Hml+Lz− numbers during larva development.
source: Their presence and integrity are necessary for the proper establishment of Hml+Lz+/Hml+Lz− numbers during larva development.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the cluster disruption experiments.

claim: The hemocytes in clusters are in dynamic relation with circulating hemocytes.
source: Interestingly, the hemocytes in clusters are in dynamic relation with circulating hemocytes (Babcock et al., 2008; Welman et al., 2010; Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cells can be observed entering circulation from the patches and leaving circulation to become sessile in video analysis.
source: This is confirmed in our videos where cells can be observed entering circulation from the patches and leaving circulation to become sessile.
evidence: This is based on video observations from the current study.

claim: Sessile plasmatocytes have a higher division rate with respect to their circulating counterparts.
source: Secondly, another interesting property of sessile plasmatocytes consists of their higher division rate with respect to their circulating counterparts (Makhijani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The existence of cell proliferation control and cell differentiation is sufficient to consider the hemocyte clusters as hematopoietic tissues.
source: We argue that the existence of these two characteristics, cell proliferation control and cell differentiation, is sufficient to consider the hemocyte clusters as hematopoietic tissues.
evidence: This is an argument based on the definition of hematopoietic tissues and the observed properties of hemocyte clusters.

claim: Hemocyte clusters enhance hemocyte proliferation and provide structure to guarantee the necessary cell contacts that engage the signaling events behind cell fate decisions.
source: In brief, hemocyte clusters enhance hemocyte proliferation and provide structure as to guarantee the necessary cell contacts that engage the signaling events behind cell fate decisions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Hemocytes in clusters can be mobilized to circulation upon immune challenge.
source: Noticeably, hemocytes in clusters can be mobilized to circulation upon immune challenge (Zettervall et al., 2004), a process that is in part dependent on the small GTPase Rac1 (Xavier and Williams, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The role of hemocyte clusters is most likely restricted to larval stages because, once pupariation starts, a peak of ecdysone promotes the dispersion of hemocytes throughout the epidermis.
source: The role of hemocyte clusters is most likely restricted to larval stages because, once pupariation starts, a peak of ecdysone promotes the dispersion of hemocytes throughout the epidermis (Regan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on citation to prior work about ecdysone effects.

claim: The differentiation of crystal cells from plasmatocytes within sessile clusters creates an interesting parallel with macrophage development in vertebrates.
source: The differentiation of crystal cells from plasmatocytes within sessile clusters creates, in our view, an interesting parallel with macrophage development in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a comparative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Macrophages are the most plastic cells in the vertebrate's hematopoietic tissue and their specialization in vivo depends on the local microenvironment provided by the tissue they colonize.
source: Macrophages are the most plastic cells in the vertebrate's hematopoietic tissue and their specialization in vivo depends on the local microenvironment provided by the tissue they colonize (Ostuni and Natoli, 2011; Wynm et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on vertebrate macrophages.

claim: In Drosophila larvae the microenvironment provided by hemocyte clusters is necessary to induce crystal cell differentiation from plasmatocytes through a cell-contact mechanism involving Notch-Serrate.
source: Similarly, here we show that in Drosophila larvae the microenvironment provided by hemocyte clusters is necessary to induce crystal cell differentiation from plasmatocytes, namely through a cell-contact mechanism involving Notch-Serrate.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: Misexpression of some genes in hemocytes can disrupt hemocyte clusters without affecting lymph gland morphology.
source: In support of this notion, misexpression of some genes in hemocytes can disrupt hemocyte clusters without affecting lymph gland morphology (Stofanko et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Throughout homeostatic development, blood cell types respect fixed relative numbers both in vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: Throughout homeostatic development, it is commonly observed, both in vertebrates (Almeida et al., 2005) and invertebrates (Rizki, 1957), that blood cell types respect fixed relative numbers.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Plasmatocytes are very plastic cells and may represent a rare case of functionally mature cells transdifferentiating into other cell types: lamellocytes and crystal cells.
source: Also, it is now evident that plasmatocytes are very plastic cells and may represent a rare case of functionally mature cells transdifferentiating into other cell types: lamellocytes (Honti et al., 2010) and crystal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current findings and citation to prior work on lamellocyte transdifferentiation.

claim: Transdifferentiation is used recurrently in cell culture assays but rarely seen in vivo.
source: Transdifferentiation, the process where a cell changes its cell fate without passing through a less differentiated state, is used recurrently in cell culture assays but rarely seen in vivo (Jopling et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.
